paper.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
paper.central_claim: Voyager, an LLM (GPT-4) agent with an automatic curriculum, a growing executable-code skill library and iterative prompting with environment feedback, execution errors and self-verification, continuously explores Minecraft, obtains 3.3x more unique items, unlocks tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster, travels 2.3x farther than prior LLM-agent baselines, and its learned skill library solves unseen tasks in a new world where baselines fail.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref not exposed to the worker; null by design (no probing).

rationale: Retained executable-skill library with LLM-critic admission; real ablations and zero-shot new-world test, but weak baselines, unaudited task overlap, no cost accounting. Retained-level, scoped.

evidence.quote: Voyager interacts with GPT-4 via blackbox queries, which bypasses the need for model parameter fine-tuning.
evidence.support_explanation: Improvement is outside weights: retained state lives in the skill library and prompts.

evidence.quote: these agents are not lifelong learners that can progressively acquire, update, accumulate, and transfer knowledge over extended time spans
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap statement: prior LLM agents lack accumulating, reusable learned skills.

evidence.quote: Each time GPT-4 generates and verifies a new skill, we add it to the skill library, represented by a vector database.
evidence.support_explanation: Persistence rule: verified skill is appended to a vector DB keyed by description embedding.

evidence.quote: Subsequently, we perform querying to identify the top-5 relevant skills.
evidence.support_explanation: Later-use rule: top-5 retrieved skills are injected into the next code-generation prompt.

evidence.quote: we instantiate another GPT-4 agent for self-verification.
evidence.support_explanation: Admission signal for a skill is an LLM critic (no ground-truth success checker).

evidence.quote: If the agent gets stuck after 4 rounds of code generation, then we query the curriculum for another task.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure handling: at most 4 rounds; unsolved tasks are re-queued by the curriculum, not stored.

evidence.quote: if the curriculum is replaced with a random one, because certain tasks may be too challenging if attempted out of order
evidence.support_explanation: Curriculum ablation (random curriculum), reported as relative drop.

evidence.quote: Voyager w/o skill library exhibits a tendency to plateau in the later stages.
evidence.support_explanation: Skill-library-off ablation: retained-library effect shown on exploration curve and tech-tree table.

evidence.quote: Removing the module leads to a significant drop
evidence.support_explanation: Self-verification-off ablation (-73% items); LLM critic is load-bearing.

evidence.quote: Fractions indicate the number of successful trials out of three total runs.
evidence.support_explanation: Main tech-tree evidence uses three trials; failures are counted (e.g. diamond 1/3 for Voyager, 0/3 for baselines).

evidence.quote: Voyager is the only one to unlock the diamond level of the tech tree
evidence.support_explanation: Headline result vs ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT (re-implemented baselines).

evidence.quote: Table. 2 and Fig. 8 show Voyager can consistently solve all the tasks, while baselines cannot solve any task within 50 prompting iterations.
evidence.support_explanation: Retained-library test: new world, cleared inventory, four unseen tasks, 3 trials each.

evidence.quote: our skill library constructed from lifelong learning not only enhances Voyager
evidence.support_explanation: AutoGPT with the learned skill library also improves; library is a transferable asset.

evidence.quote: Because there is no LLM-based agents that work out of the box for Minecraft, we make our best effort to select a number of representative algorithms as baselines.
evidence.support_explanation: Baselines are re-interpreted by the authors; ReAct/Reflexion reach 0/3 even for the wooden tool, a baseline-credibility concern.

evidence.quote: We curate 101 items obtained by Voyager and create a random curriculum by randomly selecting one item as the next task.
evidence.support_explanation: Random-curriculum control draws items from Voyager own outputs (info the baseline curriculum could not know).

evidence.quote: Occasionally, self-verification module may also fail, such as not recognizing spider string as a success signal of beating a spider.
evidence.support_explanation: Admission critic is imperfect; false negatives acknowledged, false-positive rate not measured.

evidence.quote: The GPT-4 API incurs significant costs.
evidence.support_explanation: Cost is only discussed qualitatively; no tokens/dollars per method.

evidence.quote: ReAct undergoes one round of code generation from scratch, followed by three rounds of code refinement.
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline protocol differs structurally from Voyager (no curriculum, library, retrieval); per-iteration call counts are not matched.

evidence.quote: The top-5 accuracy standing at 96.5% suggests our retrieval process is reliable
evidence.support_explanation: Retrieval evaluated on 309 samples with error bars; supports later-use step.

evidence.quote: Each question is paired with a concept that is used for retrieving the most relevant document from the wiki knowledge base
evidence.support_explanation: Curriculum gets wiki-derived context via GPT-3.5 self-ask; baselines do not get this (information asymmetry).

evidence.quote: Our approach bypasses the need for model parameter access and explicit gradient-based training or finetuning.
evidence.support_explanation: Confirms scope: non-weight harness improvement (A-class loop).

evidence.quote: We additionally run new experiments with gpt-4-0613 and find that the performance is roughly the same
evidence.support_explanation: Second GPT-4 snapshot run; only one other model version, still a single environment.

gap.author_gap: LLM agents act well but are not lifelong learners that accumulate, update and transfer skills; prior Minecraft work relies on fixed subgoals/low-level controllers.
gap.checked_gap: The fixed object is the human-written skill/primitive repertoire and the human-authored task sequence; Voyager makes the skill set (code) and the next-task choice agent-generated and persistent. The frozen-LLM framing is only background.
gap.lineage: Code-as-Policies/ProgPrompt (pre-defined skill library) -> Inner Monologue (feedback) -> Reflexion/ReAct/AutoGPT (no persistent executable skills) -> Voyager (self-generated verified skill library + curriculum).
gap.closest_adjacent: Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, Generative Agents (memory not executable), Reflexion, AutoGPT, SPRING (concurrent); LATM is concurrent and not discussed.
gap.residue: Exploration and long-horizon skill compounding in open worlds without human intervention; LLM code writing is unreliable in one shot.
gap.stakes: Prior baselines reach 0/3 on wooden tool and cannot reach diamond within 160 iterations (as reported).
gap.method_response: Persist verified programs as skills, retrieve them by description, and refine with three feedback types.
gap.remaining_gap: Skill quality control beyond the LLM critic, skill maintenance as the library grows, cost, other domains.
unresolved: nearest neighbors are cited from the paper itself; no external re-check of concurrent tool/skill libraries

G.reason: Specific fixed object (human-written skills/primitives, human-ordered tasks) and named neighbors (Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, Reflexion, AutoGPT, Generative Agents, SPRING) with a stated residual; but the claim that all neighbors lack skill libraries is asserted, and concurrent skill/tool-library work is not compared.

M.reason: Mechanism chain is explicit: practice task -> code -> three feedback types -> critic -> library -> retrieval; ablations make distinguishable predictions. Weak assumption: an LLM critic is a sufficient admission signal.

X.reason: Pseudocode, all prompts, retry limit, retrieval k and warm-up schedule are given, and limitations are stated. No deduplication, version, rollback, or deprecation of skills, and no check on skill quality beyond the critic.

E.measurement.reason: Item counts, tech-tree iteration counts, distance and zero-shot success are read from game state (objective); retrieval evaluated on 309 samples. Admission critic accuracy is not measured (reported to E.measurement as a verifier gap), baselines reaching 0/3 even for wooden tools weakens metric contrast.

E.causality.reason: Six-way ablation (curriculum, library, feedback types, critic, model) plus AutoGPT-with-library transfer. Gaps: baselines are authors re-implementations without curriculum/wiki context, random curriculum uses Voyager own items, per-iteration call budgets unmatched.

E.holdout.reason: Zero-shot tasks in a fresh world with cleared inventory separate library building from testing, but overlap of test tasks with practiced tasks is not audited, the library is the only transferred asset, and the whole study is one environment and one benchmark family.

E.statistics.reason: Three trials with mean and std, explicit failure fractions (e.g. 0/3 and 1/3 for diamond), retrieval with error bars; no confidence intervals or significance tests and ablations reported as relative drops.

E.cost.reason: GPT-4 cost is mentioned qualitatively; no token, call or dollar figures, library-building cost not separated, baselines not cost-matched.
